PROTOCOLS

From this week’s stories, 13 skills to try.

MAKE AN AGENT’S WORK EASY TO WATCH

From Alex Duffy https://every.?ev_audience=free’s “We Caught an AI Cheating by Watching It Play ‘StarCraft’” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * See what your agent is doing. Watching the match is how Alex’s team caught Astra copying code within minutes. His prompt applies that lesson to any agent: Define success up front, make its work easy to inspect, and log every attempt. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free

SET THE RULES FOR A SHARED AGENT

From Willie Williams’s “Why We Replaced Personal Agents With One for the Whole Company” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * Ask what could be undone. Engineer Will Gathright’s test: If a step is easy to undo, the agent does it and says what it assumed; if it deletes something or posts outside the conversation, it asks first. The rule https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Keep permissions out of the prompt. The Every Agent’s access rules live in code, not in its instructions, and the server checks any approval the agent claims against what the person wrote in Slack. The rule https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Keep scheduled reports running when logins change. Engineer Lee Knowlton’s fix lets any qualifying login run a scheduled report, so it keeps arriving after someone’s login expires or they leave the company. The fix https://every.?ev_audience=free

LET AGENTS CHECK THE WORK

From Laura Entis https://every.?ev_audience=free’s “Keeping Up With AI Is a Full-time Job” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * Pit two models against each other. Engineer Loren Stewart has one coding agent write a fix plan for a buggy app, another company’s agent critique it, and the first agent revise it—a sequence Arielle Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free turned into a /loren skill. The prompts https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Turn the cleanup into a scoreboard. After Railway’s security incident, Willie had Codex list every exposed credential with a likely owner, and the Every Agent posted hourly counts of what each person still had to fix. The steps https://every.?ev_audience=free

PUT YOUR DOT TO WORK

From Laura’s “Dots: A Guide for Putting OpenAI’s Always-on Agents to Work” https://every.?ev_audience=free

HAVE YOUR DOT WATCH FOR PROBLEMS

 * Put it in every channel. Kate added her Dot to all of her Slack channels and told it to be “as proactive as possible” about flagging what needs her attention. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Let it catch knock-on bugs. Loren’s Dot, which watches what he codes in other threads, warned him that a tool update would affect a colleague’s scheduled automation before it next ran. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Assign it a habit you skip. Becky Isjwara https://every.?ev_audience=free gave her Dot a communication-coach chat she kept forgetting to open, and it now reviews her meeting transcripts and sends her feedback through the day. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Call it for a briefing. While getting ready one morning, Arielle phoned her Dot, which sent her a settings link to give a colleague tool access, confirmed an event was insured, and drafted the reply. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free

GIVE YOUR DOT THE TO-DO LIST

 * Keep one conversation going. Dan no longer opens new ChatGPT threads; his Dot starts each request as its own task and messages him when the result is ready. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Correct it once, then save the rule. After Dan told his Dot not to propose evening meetings without asking, it started checking his calendar, the company calendar, and Notion and bringing him an option to approve before emailing. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Tag it in the thread. Dan tagged his Dot in a Slack thread to watch an internal app Claude was building and save the code to GitHub, and it reported back in the thread when the job was done. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free

KNOWLEDGE BASE

“Duet—Anthropic’s Always-on Agent” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free/Vibe Check https://every.?ev_audience=free: Dan was mostly a ChatGPT person until he spent two weeks with Claude Duet, Anthropic’s new always-on personal agent. Now he’s closer to 50/50 between ChatGPT and Claude. Duet is the first personal agent he’d call a pro tool: It sorts recurring topics into their own channels, tracks its tasks and what it needs from you, and keeps docs and dashboards up to date. Duet still has limitations: It can’t direct the Claude sessions it sees on your computer or use custom connections to other tools.

“Why We Replaced Personal Agents With One for the Whole Company” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Willie Williams https://every.?ev_audience=free/Source Code https://every.?ev_audience=free: In May, Willie concluded that Plus One, our personal-agent product, wasn’t working and deleted it to start afresh. We rebuilt it as the Every Agent https://every.?ev_audience=free, a shared company agent that works in Slack. Willie explains what had to change once the agent no longer belonged to any one person: following conversations involving several coworkers, keeping scheduled reports running when someone’s login expires, and putting permission rules in code so no one can talk the agent into bending them.

“We Caught an AI Cheating by Watching It Play ‘StarCraft’” https://every.?ev_audience=free by Alex Duffy/Playtesting https://every.?ev_audience=free: Alex’s Good Start Labs, which studies AI models through games, gave GPT-6 Astra https://every.?ev_audience=free and Claude Opus 5.5 https://every.?ev_audience=free 48 hours to write bots that play the strategy game StarCraft: Brood War. When Astra hit a difficult obstacle, it suddenly and very visibly changed its playstyle. Noticing this, the team checked its logs and found that Astra had gone against instructions to play fairly by copying the code of a human-built bot. YOUR AI WORKFLOW NEEDS A SCOREBOARD

Once you’ve built an AI workflow, a harder question follows: How do you know it’s getting better? Most of us change a prompt, check a few outputs, and go with our gut. In his new book from O’Reilly, Context Engineering with DSPy, Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free makes the case for measuring instead.

DSPy is an open-source framework https://every.?ev_audience=free for building AI programs you can test. You define the task, collect examples, and decide how to score the output. DSPy’s optimizers https://every.?ev_audience=free then rewrite your prompts and check whether the changes improve the score. When a new model comes out, you rerun the optimizer instead of rewriting everything by hand. The book is written for engineers building agents, but its core habit works for anyone using AI: Decide what good looks like before you start tweaking.

Buy the book from O’Reilly https://every.?ev_audience=free, then bring your questions to Mike’s livestream https://every.?ev_audience=free with Drew Breunig and DSPy lead maintainer Isaac Miller. The two cofounded Cmpnd, which builds tools for the framework, and will join Mike for a casual introduction to DSPy built around what you want to know (Thursday, October 29, 1–2 p.m. ET).

ALIGNMENT

A sting operation. An investment research firm with little biology experience helped design proteins that bind to scorpion toxins. That is a fairly extraordinary sentence to write.

The financial researchers at Citrini encountered biosecurity restrictions from Claude when attempting to work on the problem on their own, so they worked with Anthropic’s scientists at the company’s offices to use an internal research model under controlled conditions. The task was to develop the starting point for a scorpion antivenom. Claude spent about 64 hours generating and selecting protein designs—work Citrini suggests might otherwise have taken a year. Lab testing over the following months confirmed that 17 of the protein designs they found successfully bound to scorpion toxins.

Of course, this is not yet a treatment: The proteins still need to show they can neutralize toxins in cells and protect a living animal. Still, this is deeply impressive for a bunch of finance bros. If we generously assume that it crosses those hurdles, how likely is Citrini’s potential drug to become a medicine that is safe and effective for humans?

Recent research https://every.?ev_audience=free suggests it may be likelier than you think. Roughly 75 percent of AI-enabled programs at emerging biopharma companies have cleared Phase I of human trials, which is substantially higher than the rate for drug candidates developed without AI. This is the stage in which researchers assess side effects and how the body handles the drug. Phase II investigates whether the treatment really benefits patients. Here, AI programs performed roughly in line with their peers. Phase III tests treatments in larger groups to confirm benefits and assess safety, but too few AI-assisted drug programs had reached this stage to draw meaningful conclusions.

So far, AI-assisted drug development is showing signs of promise, and Citrini’s recent experiment is another encouraging sign. But while I’m extremely bullish on what AI can do for medicine, I’m not volunteering for a sting just yet.—Ashwin Sharma https://every.?ev_audience=free
